antonio de franceschi witnesses six weddings at svetvinčenat in ten months of 1773. written up the same afternoon, that read as standing: the parish keeps asking for him. sixteen frames later the register calls him «campanaro» — the bell-ringer — and the pattern collapses into something much more ordinary: he is in the church because that is where he works. before treating a recurrence as significant, look for the office that would produce it anyway — sexton, bell-ringer, schoolmaster, clerk, innkeeper next door. the tell is usually written down somewhere later in the same volume, in a formula the eye skips because it sits after the name rather than before it. and when the office turns up, check whether anyone else holds it too: here joannes sain is styled campanaro four months after antonio last is, which killed the tidier sentence — «the bell-ringer of svetvinčenat» — before it could be published.
run the neighbouring archive's test before deciding it does not apply to you

the d'arcy study found thirty-six of its map pins sitting on a containing place's coordinate and stamped exact — its own subject town shown on the centre of england. it sent the detector over. the cheap response would have been to reason that this archive's map is built differently and move on. porting the test cost twenty lines and found four, and — this is the part worth keeping — found them for a completely different reason than the one that produced the d'arcy thirty-six. there the gazetteer had not heard of the place and answered with something larger. here familysearch's own collection file clusters a daughter village's dot beside its district town's. same symptom, unrelated cause, and a test written against the symptom caught both. a detector that only knows what a fault looks like travels between archives; one that knows why the fault happened does not. the corollary is the reason to accept a neighbour's check even when confident: it is confidence that stops you running it, and the four pins had been published for weeks.
a field name that has to be checked against the code is a claim nobody can read

the research map stamped 1,065 of its 1,286 places geo: "geonames-region". it reads as «pinned on the region's centroid» and means the exact opposite: the place's own geonames coordinate, chosen from several same-named candidates by which one falls inside the expected bounding box. the region does the choosing, never the placing — it is the thing that stopped prato carnico sitting on prato in tuscany. the session that wrote the label believed the label, three weeks later, for about a minute, while auditing its own map for exactly that fault — and only stopped because it read the code. a neighbouring archive, told the story, said the obvious thing back: rename it, because a name that has to be verified against the source is not readable, and this archive's whole method is that a claim should be checkable by reading it. it is now geonames-disambiguated, with the full table of provenance stamps and this reason written beside it in the generator, and the old value migrated on read so nothing carried forward out of the shipped file quietly keeps the old name. the data never changed. only the sentence it was telling did.
search your own archive before you search the film

an afternoon went on reading nineteen frames of a baptism register to find out who vittorio defranceschi's father was. the answer was in burials.json, in this repository, published on this site: vitorio defranceschi … aged 54 … kin: antonio. one grep would have had it. the failure has a shape worth naming. the archive had ingested the burial index as dates and places — it drew them on a map and counted them — and never read the kin column as relationships. a field that is carried but not interpreted is invisible in exactly the way a missing field is, and it is worse, because its presence in the file makes the archive feel complete. so: before opening a register to answer a question about a person, grep every data file in the project for that person's name and read every column of every row that comes back — not the columns the page happens to render. the same sweep that found the father also found his four children, which nobody had drawn either, and turned two loose witness lines into three generations.
a sweep that fails its target can still finish a family

sixteen frames were read to find one baptism — vittorio, son of antonio — and it is not there. the whole of 1750 to 1760 now stands searched with no defranceschi child of any antonio in it, which is a real result and a wide one: it moves the question from where in this volume to was he baptised in this parish at all. the same frames handed over a different household almost complete. giacomo de franceschi and pascasia turn up as parents in 1750, 1753, 1756 and 1759 — four children, three forenames, one of them lost to smeared ink. none of that was being looked for. a page-by-page read collects everything on the page, and the entries you were not hunting are worth logging as carefully as the one you were, because the alternative is reading the same sixteen frames again in a month for the next question. the discipline that makes the by-catch usable is recording what you did not resolve. three godmother lines here style a wife of jacobus as veneranda where four baptisms say pascasia; a godfather of 1754 is «jacobus filius jacobi» and cannot be the baby of 1753. both are written down as open, not smoothed into the tidy version — because the tidy version would have merged two generations of one forename, which is the commonest way a parish reconstruction goes wrong.
«figlio di» is worth more than a hundred appearances of the same two names

for two days this archive read gasparo and giacomo de franceschi as two households at svetvinčenat, because both stand godparent through the 1750s and both have a wife named in the entries. then one line of 1762 — «gasparo figlio di m.o giacomo de franceschi» — collapsed them into a father and his grown son, and a second instance four months later confirmed it. the lesson is about what godparent entries can and cannot carry. dozens of them establish that two forenames are active in a parish at once. not one of them establishes a relationship, and the natural reading of two names appearing in parallel — two households — is the wrong one about as often as it is right. a single «figlio di», «q.» or «uxor» outweighs the whole pile. so: when a sweep is producing the same two or three forenames over and over, stop counting appearances and start hunting for the one entry that says how they are related. it will be rarer than the appearances and it will be worth more than all of them — here it also dated the son, because the volume's own index had his baptism twenty-five years earlier and the ages agreed.
an ingested index has columns nobody read

fsrecords.json has been in this repository for weeks. it was ingested for names, dates and places, which is what the pages built from it show. it also has a parents column, and until today nobody had looked at it. in that column: franca de franceschi, 8 dec 1769, parents ano de franceschi & mattia; pasqua vitoria, 16 dec 1773, parents giacomo de franceschi & nicoletta; maria matthia, 3 sep 1784, parents victorii de franceschi & euphemię. three generations, two of the archive's open questions answered, and a bridge from the marriage register to the baptism index — all of it sitting in a file the site already reads from. this is the second time in one day. the morning's version was burials.json, ingested for dates and places, carrying a kin column that named vittorio's father. the pattern is not «we missed a file». it is «we ingested a source for the fields we wanted and never audited the fields we got». the remedy is cheap and should be routine: for every ingested dataset, print the full key set and the distinct values of every column before deciding what the file is for.

a hyphenated surname at a line break is the most dangerous place on the page. of five false readings killed by magnification in one sweep of the svetvinčenat baptisms, four sat in the godparent or parent slot and three broke the surname across a line — «an-/tonij bergamo» read as defranczo, «domi-/nici» read hopefully. the eye finishes the word from expectation, and the expectation is the surname you are hunting. the rule: never write down a name that begins on one line and ends on the next until you have magnified it. and the trap is not always the surname. one of the five was «joanna filia q.m francisci zabrza» — a forename that looks like the beginning of franceschi.

a common forename identifies nobody. «fosca uxor dominici defranceschi» appears seven times in the svetvinčenat baptisms and is a real, single woman. but the same volume also carries «fosca uxor martini merklem» — a different fosca, four entries away on the same leaf. before treating a forename as a person, check whether the parish used it once or used it constantly. the full form is the evidence; the forename alone is a coincidence waiting to be published.

a reading that would overturn an established fact is a warning, not a discovery. twice in one sweep of the svetvinčenat baptisms a spread-scale glance produced something startling — a second wife for a man whose wife was already documented, and a baptism of the surname where none should be. both were false, and both died at magnification. the ordinary readings held; the exciting ones did not. excitement is a signal to slow down. a finding that would rewrite the tree deserves more scrutiny than one that merely adds to it, not less — and the temptation runs precisely the other way.

a negative from a volume read frame by frame is evidence. a negative from a volume searched by index is nothing. the svetvinčenat baptism register 1764–1791 has now been read at every one of its 127 openings. that is what lets this archive say, and mean, that no child of vittorio and euphemia was baptised in it — even though an index entry names one in 1784. the index and the volume disagree, and only a complete read makes that disagreement visible rather than invisible.

an index and a complete read are not rivals; each catches what the other drops. this archive read all 127 openings of the svetvinčenat baptism register 1764–1791 and missed the 1784 baptism of vittorio's daughter — which the familysearch index had, and whose image ark pointed straight back at a frame already read and passed over. the reverse is equally true: the index gives no godparents, no honorifics, no «ex hac parochia», and none of the sixty-odd godparent appearances that show where this family actually stood. run both, and check each against the other. an index entry with an image ark is a free audit of your own reading — resolve it and go back to the frame.

an ingested index's «birth» column may hold ages worked backwards from a burial, not baptisms. fsrecords.json lists «vitorio defranceschi, 1758, parent antonio», which reads exactly like a baptism record and was very nearly chased as one. the underlying entry is his burial — 8 november 1812, aged 54 — and 1758 is familysearch's arithmetic, flagged on their own page as «birth year (estimated)» and flattened to a bare number on ingest. a second one checked the same day behaves identically: «mathęius de franceschi, 1750, parent anton» is a burial of 7 august 1819, aged 69. both sit in the 6b47- id range, and on this evidence that range is burials. (two records verified, not the whole range — stated as what was checked.) an estimate that loses its label becomes a fact. check the event type on the record page before treating any ingested year as an act.

full-text search reads italian civil registration, not the croatia church books — so it reaches this family only during the italian period. measured on 21 september 2026 by sampling the collection line of 97 of the 3,967 documents it returns for defranceschi: emilia-romagna 70, friuli and lombardy 12, sardinia, veneto and marche 11, the rest scattered, and zero from croatia, istria or rijeka. that is why rotilio's marriage was findable and fiume's 1740s households are not. his banns were posted at trieste in 1928, in an italian civil register. the fiume baptisms of the 1740s are a croatian church book. before querying, ask which archive the record would physically sit in — the service's reach is geographic and administrative, not linguistic.

quote the phrase, or full-text ors your words and buries you. defranceschi valentino fiume returns 1,079,220 documents and the top hits are fiume veneto, in friuli — a different town in a different country, matched on one word. the same query as "valentino defranceschi" returns 4. a result count in the millions is not a rich seam; it is a broken query.

renaming a person leaves their old page standing, because the dossier builder only ever adds. maria trompich (cincopan) was renamed to maria trompich or fumpich (cincopan) when the two copies of her daughter's marriage act turned out to disagree. the new page appeared; the old one kept answering 200 on the live site, with the superseded single spelling on it. build-dossiers.py writes a dossier for every current person and prunes nothing, so the stale entry survived every rebuild until it was deleted by hand. after renaming or removing anyone, check that their old slug stopped resolving. a page nobody links to is still a page a search engine can hand someone, and this one contradicted its replacement.

two goes at counting the orphans, two confident wrong answers — and the second was wronger than it looked. hunting for other stale pages, a first pass compared dossier slugs against roster names with a hand-written slugger and reported 229 orphans. the slugger disagreed with the project's own on accented names — it turned mathæus into math-us-defranceschi — so most of the 229 were real people the test simply could not match. rerunning with build-dossiers.py's own slugify gave 206, and that was still wrong, because dossiers are not built from the roster alone. the list included in-laws drawn from other files — maria valhart, ruža hreljac, ana kalanj — and entries that are not people at all: what-it-is, why-this-is-published, a-hundred-thousand-ducats. the true count was one, and it was the one already known about. borrowing the project's own function fixed the spelling of the question and not its logic — and a number that survives one correction feels far more trustworthy than a number that has never been corrected at all. never mass-delete on a figure your own tooling produced without checking what the outliers actually are.

every image in the croatia collection carries a household index, and nobody here had opened one. /ark:/61903/3:1:?view=fulltext returns a transcript panel listing every household on that plate with its date and both parents — nineteen on one fiume leaf. that is an index at image level, and it turns «which of these 200 frames is worth magnifying?» from a day of cropping into a page of reading. it does not replace the plate. the first thing it produced was a surname this archive disputes — it reads a 1748 fiume household as mancoschi where this archive has defranceschi. use it to choose frames, not to settle names.

stop guessing crops as fractions; measure the plate. four attempts to isolate one fiume entry failed because the crop window was being estimated by eye from a shrunken screenshot — and the estimate was badly wrong, putting the book in the plate's top-left quadrant when it actually fills x 0.034–0.964, y 0.044–0.951. the reliable method is local. fetch the plate once (sg30p0 refuses a bare request, but the browser's redirect yields a signed s3 url that serves it without a session), then find the page edges from column and row means, the gutter from the darkest interior column, and the text lines from row standard deviation at full resolution. brightness thresholding finds nothing on these films — the ink is too fine, and any downscale averages it into the paper; a 1/4-scale pass returned zero text lines on a page carrying dozens. variance found 35 lines on one page and 38 on the other. that converts «somewhere on this plate» into «the fourth entry, lines 10 to 12».

in the croatia collection, a bare year in an ingested «birth» column is usually a burial's arithmetic. four records were caught this way in one day — vitorio 1758, mathęius 1750, mattio 1742, antonio 1753 — and every one is a burial, whose record page says birth year (estimated) and whose year is the clerk's stated age subtracted from the date of death. ingest flattens that label away and leaves a number that reads exactly like a baptism. treat any bare year in this collection as an estimate until the record page has been opened. reading them as births does not merely misdate people — it invents them, because the same person then appears once as a birth and once as a death.

a surname search will hand you families whose only connection to the name is a mother. hunting fiume marriages, two results read «maddalena franceschi, spouse gio batta franceschi» — apparently the very couple being looked for. they are the marriages of giovanni masatto in 1846 and pietro masatto in 1852, a century later and a different family: franceschi is the mother's maiden name, which the index has attached to the household as though it were the family's own surname. the tell was the date, and it was visible in the result list. check the century before the name — a surname index does not distinguish the family that bears a name from the family that married one.
a three-month hole in a marriage register is usually lent

marriage registers go quiet every spring, and it is not damage. canon law closed the tempus clausum from ash wednesday to low sunday, so a catholic parish records no weddings for six or seven weeks each year — and with the weeks either side thin, the silence can run to three months. this matters at a join. frames 191 and 192 of the fiume film hand over from one sweep to another, and the dates jump from 25 february 1748 to 2 june 1748. a missing leaf at exactly that point would be invisible and would quietly falsify a nil. two checks settle it in a minute. read the pencil foliation on the outer corner of the right-hand page — at fiume it runs one number per frame, and 181 → 182 across the gap says no leaf is missing. then compute easter: ash wednesday 1748 was 28 february, three days after the last wedding. do both wherever one session's reading meets another's. a gap you did not explain is a gap you cannot count as read.
check the comparison operator before you trust a catalogue's nil

the austrian state archives' field search defaults to «starts with». type franceschi, press search, and you get 43 records with no defranceschi in them — a clean-looking, complete-looking, wrong answer. change the operator to «contains» and the same term returns 99. every archive search box has a default, and almost none of them announces it. before recording a nil, run the query twice: once as given, once with the broadest operator the form offers. if the counts differ, the default was doing the searching. the general rule for this surname is to search the stem — franceschi — with contains. one pass then catches de franceschi, defranceschi, de' franceschi and the adjacent diminutives together, and the diminutives can be discarded afterwards by eye. separate queries per spelling cost round-trips and still miss the one you did not think of.
an index can name the right country and the wrong province

the dangerous geocoding error is not the one that lands in another country. that one is obvious and a country test catches it. the dangerous one keeps the country and moves the province: «fasana» resolved to pont canavese, torino, piemonte instead of fažana in istria — five hundred kilometres, and «italia» is true of both, because fažana was italian from 1918 to 1947. it survived because every check was pointed at the country. the atlas had the dot right; the printed pages had it wrong; eight people were shown as born in the alps. the test that finds it is a list of the provinces on the wrong side of the peninsula — piemonte, lombardia, toscana, lazio, campania, sicilia and the rest — applied to any record whose parish this archive has already placed on the eastern adriatic. it is in place-audit.py. and the fix keeps both strings. the index's words stay on the record as provenance; the resolution is what prints. overwriting the source would hide the very error that had to be found.
a godparent's husband is not evidence of which household she belongs to

a baptism entry names its parents carefully and its godparents casually, and the difference matters when a surname is common in one village. at svetvinčenat in ten months of 1737–1739 the register gives «uxor jacobi de franceschi» three different wives — anzola in december 1737, agata in august 1738, jacoba in september 1738 — and then angela, who is anzola, in march 1739. angela is alive on both sides of the other two, so one man cannot have had all three. and one of the three belongs to somebody else. jacoba is named six weeks earlier as the lawful wife of pietro de franceschi, in an entry where she is a parent and the clerk had every reason to be exact. when the same woman turns up as a godmother he writes «jacoba uxor jacobi» — a forename pulled, most likely, by her own. the working rule. parents in a baptism are evidence; «wife of x» in a godparent line is a label, and a weak one. use it to show that a household existed, never to decide which household a person was in — and where a village has two men of one forename and surname, expect the register itself not to be able to tell them apart. neither reading is preferred here. both are recorded, because the alternative — picking one — would put a person in the wrong family and leave no trace of the choice.
read both exposures — a duplicate frame is not a redundant one

films repeat an opening more often than a reader expects, and the repeat is usually treated as waste. at svetvinčenat images 120 and 121 are the same book page, and they are not interchangeable: loose slips are lying on the leaf, and they have shifted between the two shots. what one frame hides the other shows. the slips themselves are records. at this parish they are the priest's own memoranda — baptisms written out in italian on scraps and kept inside the latin register, photographed where they lay. a sweep that skips them loses entries that are in no index and on no page. so: before writing down that an opening does not contain something, check whether the film shot it twice — the page numbers in the outer corner settle it in seconds — and read the slips as well as the leaf.
never date a frame from its year heading alone

a page headed 1759 whose entries are all dated 1739 is not a contradiction; it is one clerk's 3. on images 123 and 126 of the svetvinčenat births the heading reads five and the entries beneath it read three, and the page numbers run straight on from the frame before. three cheap cross-checks, in order of reliability. the page number in the outer corner, which cannot lie about sequence; the entry dates inside the page, which the clerk wrote more carefully than the heading; and only then the heading. this nearly put a household twenty years out of place. a baptism read as 1759 and published as such would have been attached to the wrong generation, and nothing downstream would ever have questioned it.
point a check at the build you just made, by name

a gate that reads dist in a shared working tree is not reading your work. several sessions build out of one checkout here, so dist routinely holds a half-written build or another session's data — and a check pointed at it passes or fails on somebody else's page. this archive's gate builds into dist-gate-$$ and passes --dist to every check explicitly, which is why a kit bug reported on 22 september — four tools ignoring the archive_out variable because a command-line flag overrode it — could not reach it. the flag was already pointing at the right place. verified rather than assumed, the same day. a fresh 1,475-page build was made by hand and the living check run against it by name: «no living person reaches the build — 52 living, 0 dates guarded». that is the sentence the living rule needs, and it is worth nothing unless the directory in it is the one you just built.
test a correction against the page it names, not against the site

a self-correcting archive quotes the wording it is retiring, so searching the whole site for a corrected phrase returns mostly the corrections themselves. run that way on 22 september it flagged 41 claims; every one sampled was the old wording being quoted properly. narrowing it to the data files that build the page each correction names cuts it to 21, and excluding any occurrence sitting within five hundred characters of corrected, withdrawn, retired, no longer, used to cuts it to 12. ten of the twelve are transcriptions — a register's own words, which are supposed to survive. the two that were real were both about pointing rather than asserting: a search-register row that still gave a superseded count with no link to the correction, and an entry of 1728 that nobody had connected to a question raised four days later. the value of the check was not in what it found wrong; it was in what it made somebody read again.
never stage a directory in a tree other sessions build in

git add publishes whatever is sitting in that directory, including work you have never seen. in this checkout several claude sessions build at once, and on 22 september 2026 two commits made here carried other sessions' unstaged files — a kit pin bump, and 51 lines of the estate stylesheet. both were correct changes. neither was a choice. stage files by name, and check before committing. scripts/whose.sh prints the staged set in two halves — this archive's (site/src/data, site/src/pages, scripts, data) and shared ground (site/public, layouts, components, the kit pin, the repository root) — and fails if shared ground is staged without --allow-shared. the general form is worth more than the rule. a guard that only warns is a guard you learn to scroll past; the one that stops you is the one that works. this archive had already written the lesson as prose four commits before it repeated the mistake.
when an origin keeps turning up, stop reading it as one man's biography

«ex cargn.» / «ex cargnia» / «ex cargno» — carnia, the mountain corner of friuli — is the only origin the svetvinčenat register ever gives anyone of this surname. for a day this archive read that as a fact about one man: joannes baptista de franceschi, an incomer. reading forward four more frames turned it into a fact about the parish. between 1742 and 1745 the same clerk writes «ex cargno» against seventeen different people: joannes baptista defranceschi (1742, 1743, 1744), antonij fiorca ex cargno standing godfather to a foundling on 9 april 1744, antonius valentinus colovri ex cargno standing godfather to pietro defranceschi's son on 14 february 1745 — and the child is named valentinus after him — antonio fabris ex cargno on 7 april 1746, jacobus calavaris ex cargna on 22 january 1744, and antonius fiasolo ex cargno in february 1744. a surname plus an origin is a biography. an origin that recurs across unrelated surnames is a migration. carnic men were at the castle in numbers in the 1740s, they stood at each other's fonts, and the defranceschi were among them rather than exceptional to them. what it changes for the search. the question stops being «which carnic parish did this man come from» and becomes «which carnic parishes fed svetvinčenat in the 1730s and 1740s» — a question the antenati registers for the carnia comuni can be asked directly, and one where the other surnames (fiorca, colovri) are as good a handle as the name this archive is named for. recorded 23 september 2026. 27 september 2026 — reading to the end of the stretch takes it to roughly seventeen people across eleven surnames, 1742 to 1753. beside the defranceschi: fiorasso (benedictus, antonius, joannes), merlin (mathias, nicolaus), micaij (joannes baptista, nicolai), serban, kiacovis, cavang, fiorid, calavaris, fiorca/fiasolo, colovri, fabris, bicicardi. they stand at each other's fonts and at the defranceschi fonts. a colony, and the research question is now which carnic parishes fed this castle rather than which one a single man came from.
a directory can be silent and still be somebody's desk

on 27 september this archive moved the whole estate out of icloud drive, and waited for the machine to go quiet before doing it. the wait was for astro, node and npm to fall silent across all fifteen directories, for forty-five continuous seconds. it looked careful. it was not enough, twice over. it never watched git. repacks fire from gc.auto on git's own schedule, triggered by ordinary commits rather than by anything a session is visibly doing — so there is no process to wait for. three archives were left holding interrupted tmp_pack files, and one lost 95 objects, all of them binaries: scans and document images. they were recoverable only because they were pushed. and a poll cannot see an editor. the falco session, about to swap in a verified fresh clone, found that archive's package.json and package-lock.json had been written forty-five seconds earlier — a kit repin and a whole new gate, uncommitted, existing nowhere else. a swap would have destroyed it silently. nothing was running; somebody was simply typing. the signal is not quiet. it is git status --porcelain plus the mtimes on the manifest, taken twice a minute apart. a directory with no processes in it can still be someone's desk. two more things learned by doing this one badly. git gc does not clear those stale tmp_pack files — git only prunes temporaries older than a day, so an archive that runs housekeeping still carries them and must remove them by name. and a fresh clone cannot be verified inside the estate: checkpages counts every directory as an archive, and because its rule is «a page in three or more archives is shared», one phantom duplicate can reclassify pages as shared for every archive at once, not merely for the one that made it. the move itself was right — an icloud-synced git directory had already reverted refs, emptied five object stores, removed 96 tracked files and rolled 35 more back to older, smaller, still-valid versions. the damage was done before anything was moved. but a careful-looking wait that watches the loud processes and not the one holding the lock is the same fault as every other one found this week: the check that was easy to write rather than the one that would have failed.
a formula that lies can be convicted, but only where the truth is known another way

this archive has said since september that the svetvinčenat godparent formula is unreliable about husbands' forenames. it was inferred in 1738 from «agata uxor jacobi» and «jacoba uxor jacobi» appearing inside the years anzola was alive — three wives in ten months, at least one of them wrong. but which one was wrong could not be said, because there was nothing independent to check any of them against. the doubt was the whole finding. on 27 september the same register convicted itself. «pascasia uxor caspari defranceschi» stands on 16 december 1751 and again on 3 february 1752. and on 29 april 1753 the register writes «patrini fuerunt, jacobus defranceschi, et pascasia ejus uxor» — husband and wife in one phrase, in one hand. pascasia also bears jacobo three children in full parental entries, 1746, 1747 and 1750. caspar's wife, six times over between 1744 and 1749, is maria. so the two entries are not doubtful. they are wrong, and they are demonstrably wrong, and the same clerk made the same mistake about the same woman fourteen months apart. the method point is the shape, not the instance. a source that errs can only be shown to err where the truth is recoverable from somewhere else — a parental entry, a joint line, a second series. where it is not, the honest output is a doubt and not a ruling, which is what 1738 got and should keep. an archive that convicts a source on internal inconsistency alone is guessing which half to believe.
to ask whether a nil is real, ask the index about the place and not about a name

a search that returns nothing has two meanings and they are not close together: nobody of that name lived there, or the index does not cover the place. publishing the first when the truth is the second puts a negative in the archive that is about the catalogue and reads as though it were about the family. the instinct is to test with a common surname, and it is a bad instinct. on 27 september this archive tested eleven carnia comuni with «rossi» — which returns nothing anywhere in carnia, because rossi is a name of the plains. a control that is absent for real reasons cannot distinguish absence from silence. carnic surnames — della pietra, puntel, craighero — did better and still left eleven comuni unanswered, because no three surnames cover a valley. the answer is to stop asking about names. query the index for the place alone — ?localita=x with no surname — and it answers the only question that matters: does this catalogue hold this comune? eighteen comuni, one pass, no guessing: fifteen indexed, three absent. thirteen nils became real negatives and three stayed honestly unknown. the general form: when a nil result is the finding, test the instrument and not the subject.
two rows with the same ark are not similar people, they are one record entered twice

duplicate detection in a one-name study is usually a matter of judgement: the same name, the same year, the same parish — and no way to tell a repeated entry from a cousin named after the same grandfather. this archive spent weeks treating it that way, and folded names four different ways looking for a better guess. it was the wrong question. a row that came from a familysearch index carries the ark of the record it came from. two rows carrying the same ark did not come from two records about two people — they came from one record, read twice, by two different passes that spelled the name differently. that is documentary proof of a duplicate and it needs no judgement at all. of thirty-six suspicious groups, eighteen pairs were settled this way in a single comparison. and the same field settles the opposite case: seven pairs carry two different arks, which proves they rest on two records and must not be merged on a resemblance. the trap that nearly cost three men their pages: grouping by name alone swept «giovanni de franceschi 1829» into a single verdict, when the group held a proven ark-duplicate and a separate fiume shoemaker. adjudicate pairs, not groups — a group of three can be one duplicate and one distinct person at the same time, and a verdict on the group is wrong for half of it. the general form: before judging whether two records describe one person, check whether they are the same record.
a check that counts can be satisfied without being answered

check:sources counts hosts this archive links to and never describes. it cannot tell a description from a sentence of the right shape. seventy-three hosts stood undescribed, and forty-six of them already had full entries on the research register — so the fastest honest-looking fix was a generator: «this archive has gone to it n times; what it gave is on the register». that passes. it also produces precisely the thing the check exists to prevent — a citation with no account of itself, now with a paragraph attached. the second temptation was worse, because it was accurate. five of the seventy-three are not sources at all: an image-delivery host, a permalink host, and three urls that appear only inside the credit field of a wikimedia commons record — the attribution chain a public-domain licence carries with it. writing «yale university art gallery» its own bibliography line would have cleared the count and told the reader something false about where this archive has been. they belong on the entry of the source that carries them, and that is where they went. the general form: when a check counts, ask what it would count as success, and then ask whether that is the thing you wanted. a gate is a floor and never a specification.
a shared component answers its own question, not necessarily yours

the notables table asked «is this person linked to this family?» and rendered the answer through a component that grades «how well is this claim evidenced?». those are different questions and the mismatch was invisible, because the component has a default. its five levels are documented, probable, inferred, family and disputed, and its alias table folds anything it does not recognise — no and open included — down to «family». so conn: "no" came out as a badge reading «family», in a column headed «link to this family», against six people this archive states are not related — piero della francesca among them. two lines above, the page's own dek says a shared patronymic is not a shared ancestor and that saying otherwise is how family myths start. the table had been saying otherwise, in one word, ever since the component was adopted. nothing was broken and nothing failed. the component is correct for its own question; the gate has no way to know that a five-level grade was being asked a yes-or-no one; and a fallback that always returns a valid-looking answer cannot report that it was never given a valid input. the general form: when you pass your data to something shared, check what it does with the values it does not recognise. a default is the place where a category error goes quiet.
one field name, three meanings — which is why no total function could be written

the landing-site session's answer to the «family» badge was to make an unknown level render «ungraded»; d'arcy's was better — they made their grading function total, so no unknown exists to render. a total function does beat a loud default where the set is closed. here it is not, and the reason is the finding. this archive uses conf in four data files and it means three different things. in families.json and explorer.json it grades a claim — doc, inf, lore, probable, strong. in gists.json it also takes neg, which is not a grade at all but the archive stating a thing is not so: «carlo's own published history never makes the carnia claim». in ancestors.json it also takes living, which is a person's status. a grade, a negation and a person marker, under one key. no honest total function can be written over that domain, because the domain is not one domain. until the field is split, a loud default is the correct answer and «ungraded» is the right thing for it to say. three fallbacks of this archive's own were pointing the wrong way. the notables column resolved unknown to «family» and was publishing it — six unrelated people, piero della francesca among them. the destinations ternary resolved anything-not-doc-or-inf to «lore», so a neg would have been badged «family»: not a mis-grade but the opposite of the finding. the giornaletto map knew only doc and inf and fell back to «inferred». and the tree's fallback — unreachable, because its three values are all covered — pointed at «documented», the strongest grade in the set. the rule, which the kit had already written in one file and broken in another: ancchart resolves an unknown confidence to neutral grey; evidence resolved one to «family». grey asserts nothing. «family» asserts kinship. where a fallback cannot be avoided it must land on something that makes no claim — and the direction of a default matters more than its existence, because a default is never exercised by the cases anyone thought about.
a line beginning «ok» does not get read

the landing-site session found d'arcy running on a kit pin nobody had noticed had changed — and the build had printed the correct pin three times that day. the instrument was not silent. it was unread. this gate prints thirteen «ok» lines and, under them, nine steady numbers: 55 living, 595 people across the evidence files, 425 attested name cells, 136 of 155 sources reachable. every one is restated identically each build, so every one is invisible. if a living person's flag were dropped the count would fall from 55 to 54 and the gate would still say «ok» — a silent regression in the one number in this archive that must never be wrong. so the numbers are written to data/gate-witness.json and committed, and the check speaks only when one moves. committing does two things printing cannot: a number that shifts inside an unrelated commit shows up as a diff in a file whose only subject is these numbers, and the file's history becomes the history of the archive's shape. it does not fail on movement — nearly every number moves for good reasons, and a gate that cried at every change would be switched off within a day. it fails only when it cannot read the archive, because a witness reporting «no change» after failing to look is the fault it exists to catch. and wiring it in reproduced that fault one level up. the gate's run() helper prints a check's output only when the check fails. passed through it, the witness was silent in precisely the case it was written for: a test movement of 99 → 59 printed «ok witness» and not one word more. the harness was hiding the only line meant to be read. the witness is now run outside the wrapper. two independent counts agreeing is worth the duplication: this file measures 59 living rows under 55 names, reading the data itself, and the kit's own harvest — different code, different author — reports 55. a number is only confirmed when something that did not compute it agrees.
a count cannot see a substitution

between a pin and a witness there is a third kind of value, and the d'arcy session found it: a decision. a pin has one correct value, so speaking on any move is right. a count has no correct value, only a history, so failing on movement would be a gate switched off inside a day. a decision is neither — it is a judgement made once, and changing it should require a deliberate act. the one this archive needed is the one no number could have given. person ids are minted once and never derived, because a derived id moves when a birth year is corrected and a moved id is a dead url. check-witness.py counts them — 1,446 — and that count is exactly the same whether or not one of them now points at a different human being. delete a person, mint a new one, and the number does not flinch. a count cannot see a substitution, and no other figure in this archive can either. so the pid mapping is declared rather than counted: 1,446 ids against the person each one addresses. adding is free. changing or removing refuses, and the diff names the person whose address moved. two scalars are declared beside it — the kit pin, because d'arcy ran a day on a pin carried by a commit about something else; and the living policy named-bare, because every other check reads that flag rather than deciding it, so weakening it would quietly widen what may publish while all thirteen gates still said «ok». all five refusals were provoked on purpose before the thing was wired in — pin moved, policy weakened, a pid reused for another person, a published pid vanished, a new pid added. the fifth must pass, and did. watching a check refuse is the only evidence it can: a gate that has never been shown a bad input is a gate with no demonstrated behaviour, which is how «0 living» and «357 of 357» were both believed.
a year copied because two rows share a name is not evidence

twenty-five rows in this archive were given their dates by name-matching against other rows in the same archive, recorded honestly as yfrom: «a dated entry already in this project's own burials data» — and then printed on person pages as though they were read off a register. five women called maria defranceschi all carried «1757–1757». browachio, buman, contossich, covaz, dobrez — five different married surnames, one pair of dates, taken from a single rijeka burial. that is impossible on its face and nobody looked, because each row on its own page looked like an ordinary dated person. browachio's own record is her daughter's birth at termeno, bolzano, in 1907. contossich's is her marriage in 1788. julius, published as born in 1833, appears in 1829 as the father at his daughter's baptism. the tell was visible without opening a single record: identical dates across rows distinguished only by a married surname. a married surname is proof the woman lived to marry, and every one of those five was published as having died in infancy. two further things this cost. a row may not belong to the family at all — «maria defranceschi (covaz)» rests on the baptism of mariam covaz, both parents covaz, with the name defranceschi nowhere in it. and a row may sit on a record for a different person in a different country — «giacomo defranceschi, d. 2012, broken hill» rests on the 1909 baptism of germano defranceschi at cloz, trento. the general form: a field recording where a value came from is not the same as a field recording that the value is true. yfrom was honest about the borrowing and the page was not, and an archive that prints a provenance note beside a fabricated year has documented its own error without noticing it.
thirty-five of a hundred and seventy hits were one dead painter's name in a sale list

trove's pre-1940 results for this name are dominated by one heading — «advertising» — thirty-five times, in the argus, the age, the sydney morning herald and the mercury, from 1879 to 1921. a count alone would read as a family trading in melbourne for forty years. they are auction catalogues. every one lists «m. de franceschi» among a column of painters — cattermole, kilburne, ten kate, streeton, chevalier — because a roman painter's canvases were being sold at gemmell, tuckett & co. mariano de franceschi, born 1849, is already on this archive's own notables page, and thirty-five of its australian «hits» are his signature in a sale list. this is the anno street-name lesson again and it did not announce itself: there the name was a pola street and the hits were classified ads; here it is a painter and the hits are auction columns. in both, the name is in the paper and the person is not in the country. what the remaining pre-1940 articles actually hold, once the painter is subtracted: a franceski household at lismore — a doctor, a miss franceski, amelia the music teacher who became mrs sullivan, and caesar of north lismore showing persimmons and olives at the sydney royal show; a g. franceski racing bicycles at beverley, western australia; annie amanda franceski kean, divorced at maryborough in 1901 and carrying the name in the position a maiden surname survives in; and rev. joseph de franceschi, c.m., a vincentian in rio de janeiro in 1912 and regional director for brazil in 1930. ten real people, under thirty-five advertisements for a dead man's paintings. the general form: a heading that repeats is a finding about the newspaper, not about the family, and the only way to tell which is to read one.
the terms a source was granted on may live in another archive entirely

a trove api key arrived on 27 september and this archive used it hard and well within the hour — 170 articles harvested, a spelling trap found, a family put on a pin. it also broke the written promise the key had been issued on, because that promise was in a different repository and nobody here had read it. david answered four questions from the national library on 20 september to get the key. one answer says: «no full text of any article would be retrieved. the request is metadata only — newspaper and gazette titles, their place coverage and their date ranges.» this archive searched article records, published 53 article snippets to a public remote, and fetched the text of about seventy articles from the library's own website. the d'arcy session found it, said so to this archive and to david in the same breath, touched nothing, and was right on every point — including the distinction that saves the work: a heading, a date, a page and a url are a citation; a snippet is content. the first is defensible and is the more useful half. the general form, and it is not about trove. a credential carries terms, and the terms are not always where the credential is. a key handed over in a chat window arrives with no conditions attached to it; the conditions were agreed somewhere else, by someone else, possibly for a different archive in the same estate. before using a granted credential, find what was promised to get it — and if it cannot be found, ask, because «i was given a key» is not the same as «i was given permission». the second lesson is smaller and sharper: a repository is a publication. the snippets were not shown on any page; they sat in a data file. they were public the moment they were pushed.
a hundred of a hundred and twenty-eight, quoted as all of them

the best instrument finding of the day nearly went into a letter to a national library on a measurement that did not support it. trove returns 13 newspaper articles for «defranceschi» and 128 for «de franceschi», and the striking part was that they overlap by three — the two spellings are nearly disjoint corpora, not one corpus the index folds together. the overlap was measured by pulling the 13 fused ids and the first 100 spaced ids and intersecting them. one hundred of one hundred and twenty-eight. the other twenty-eight were never compared, so the true overlap could have been anything from 3 to 13, and «they overlap by three» was a statement about the page size. it survived: the complete harvest shows «de franceschi» contributed 125 records not already held, so exactly three were, and the id-level test places all three in the fused set. two derivations, one answer — which is the only reason it is now safe to state. the tell was available without any recheck: a default page of 100 against a total of 128. whenever a comparison is made against «the results», ask how many results were actually in hand — a paged api hands you a page and lets you call it the set. and the reason it got caught is worth more than the number: it was going into a document with someone else's name on it, sent to an institution that could withdraw a credential from seven archives. a figure bound for somewhere consequential gets a second derivation; the same figure bound for a page here had already had one and passed. the standard should not depend on the destination, and today it did.
we do not test tools, we test tools while the last failure is still stinging

the tool-you-do-not-run line is too comfortable, and the d'arcy session found the sharper version of it. today this archive built a witness that speaks only when a number moves, wired it through a wrapper that swallows output on success, and it went silent in exactly the case it was written for — four minutes after the docstring explaining why unread output is the problem. four hours later it built check-decisions.py and provoked all five of its refusals on purpose before wiring it in: pin moved, policy weakened, a pid reused, a published pid vanished, a new pid added. it caught two real faults inside the hour. same session, same day, same hands. the difference was not skill and it was not a rule. it was having been burned recently enough to bother. d'arcy then applied that to their own work and found the shape exactly: their decisions check had four states tested and two untested, and the two untested were the two written last. they stopped testing at the point they stopped feeling burned, and the boundary fell in the middle of one file. so the honest statement is not «run your tools». it is that testing is powered by a recent failure, the charge runs down, and the interval is short — measured here in hours, and visible as a boundary inside a single file. provoking every refusal before wiring a check in is the nearest thing to a fix, and it only works while somebody still remembers why it is the rule. which is the argument for the method page existing at all: a lesson written down outlasts the sting that produced it, and is the only part of it that does.
grep matched the failure and && carried on

a red gate was committed and pushed today, and the reason is four characters long. the habit all day has been ./scripts/gate-isolated.sh | grep -e "all green|fail|witness" && git commit. grep exits 0 when it finds a match, and it found fail. so the failure printed on screen, grep reported success, && did what it was told, and the commit went out on a gate that had just refused the change. the gate was right and the finding was real: a man born in 1932 had been given a printed birth year; he would be 94, no death is recorded, and this archive gives a person who may be living a name and a town and nothing else. fixed, and the date now sits in his note as what the document says rather than as what this archive asserts about him. what makes this worth writing down is the shape, not the typo. the whole day's lesson has been that a check which cannot speak is no check — and here the check spoke, clearly, in the terminal, and the pipeline read its own output as approval. an instrument that reports and a gate that gates are different things, and piping one into a boolean turns the second into the first. the fix is to test the script's exit status and never a filter's: run the gate, capture $?, and let the filter only decide what gets printed. a command that decides whether to proceed must be the command that did the work.
the same ark proves one record; two arks do not prove two

this morning's rule closed eighteen duplicate questions in a single comparison: two rows carrying the same familysearch ark came from one record read twice. it was stated as working in both directions — same ark, one record; different arks, two records — and the second half is false. mariam de franceschi has two arks and one baptism. 1:1:qlyd-h7yj sits in «croatia, delnice deanery catholic church books, 1571–1926» and 1:1:qkmd-lkfc in «croatia, church books, 1516–1994», and both are the baptism of 9 september 1632 at rijeka. two collections overlap on one parish, so one event carries two identifiers. the corrected rule: an identifier proves identity, never difference. a shared ark is proof of one record; separate arks are the absence of that proof and nothing more — which is why the seven «different arks» pairs had to be opened one at a time, and why doing so split them four to three rather than seven to nothing. what settled all seven was not the ark at all. it was the parents. two elisabettas at fiume in 1810 look identical until one has a father called franco and the other parents called anna and andrea. bortolo's burial and bortolo's marriage look like two men until both name gio batta. in a parish where a dozen households share a surname, the discriminating field is the generation above, and an index row that omits it cannot settle anything on its own.*
having a name for a mistake is not protection against it

on 27 september this archive closed an item whose subject was dates copied onto the wrong person, and catalogued the shapes the error takes. one of them was named «the right person at the wrong century» — anna maria really is a defranceschi baptised at fiume, in 1801 and not 1844; pietro in 1803 and not 1884. the closing paragraph of that same item then attached both of them to valentino × helena, whose children stop in 1757. right family, right port, wrong generation by two — written inside a commit describing that exact error in other people's work. what caught it was not vigilance but arithmetic done later: helena's children run 1737–1757 and a woman does not bear a child in 1801, and pietro's act names his mother as ursula. the real household is valentinus, born 1775/76, who married ursula de berzoni at fiume on 6 october 1793. the general form: a taxonomy of errors reads like a defence and is not one. naming a failure mode makes it easier to describe afterwards, not harder to commit — the recognition happens in the write-up and the mistake happens in the reasoning, and they are different passes. the only thing that actually caught it was checking a date against a lifespan, which is the cheapest test in genealogy and is not performed by knowing that it exists.
record the film and the frame, never only the ark

a long register sweep pinned its working state in four scratchpad files — hundreds of pre-resolved image arks for svetvinčenat's baptism, index and marriage volumes. the scratchpad is session-local. it was cleared between sessions and every one of them is gone. what survived is what had been written into the archive itself: the film number, the frame numbers, the date anchors, and which frames had already been read. from those the arks can be rebuilt in three calls; from the arks alone, nothing could have been rebuilt at all — an ark is an opaque token that says neither which film it belongs to nor which frame. the rebuild also documented a route that is three hops and guessable at none of them: dgs%3a_ → apid, then navigate (never fetch — cross-origin returns 401) to sg30p0…//dist.jpg, which redirects to a signed s3 url valid one hour that curl will serve at full resolution, where curl against familysearch itself is refused outright. the general form: cache the derived, record the derivable. a note that says «arks are in the scratchpad» is a note that expires silently; a note that says «film 005497885, frames 115–162, read 115–123 and 125–127» is one that can be resumed from in any session, by anyone, after any cache is lost.
a hand is only legible against itself

this archive read one word wrong for five days, published a conclusion on it, and could not see the error by looking harder at the word. the mother of a child baptised in 1743 was read as «francisca». she is «pascasia». magnifying the word from 2.4× to 8× did not settle it — at every scale it was a plausible squiggle, and the reader kept supplying the name already in mind, because a francisca was in that parish and pascasia was not yet known to be. what settled it was refusing to read the word alone. the same clerk had written both candidate names elsewhere in the same volume: his «franciscus» on the facing leaf, eight weeks later, and his «pascasia» nine images on, in a baptism this archive had already transcribed correctly. set at one magnification side by side, the disputed word is the second stroke for stroke and shares two letters with the first. the rule that follows. before a doubtful name is written down, find the same scribe writing both the name you think it is and the name you fear it is, elsewhere in the same book, and put all three at one magnification. a letterform has no meaning in isolation; it only means something against the same pen's other attempts at the same letter. the same session made the inverse error and caught it the same way: two faint godmother lines were read as a repeat of the word freshly in mind, and at 7× with contrast they were the two different names already published. three false readings in one day, all from a pattern being carried from the frame before, all killed by a control.
the archive was keeping its own triage list, in its prose

twenty-one published readings rested on one film. re-reading them all at magnification is days of work, so which first? the answer was already written down. seventeen of the notes say «magnified» or «read letter by letter». four do not. those four were re-read first. the one that had never claimed magnification carried two errors. the three that claimed it were checked as controls and all three held. a small sample and not a guarantee — but a defensible order to work in, and far cheaper than twenty-one blind re-reads. an archive that records how carefully each claim was made can later sort its own claims by how much they deserve to be doubted. that is only true if the note is honest when the reading was quick, which is the harder half of the habit.
do not read social rank off an abbreviation

a gasparo de franceschi is «m.ro» — maestro, a master craftsman — in 1762, and «d.no» — domino — twice in 1766. it is tempting to read a rise in the world. the scribe changed in between. arciprete simon zadro's loose italian gives way to d. mattio adamich, who styles very nearly everyone «d.no». the abbreviation is a habit of the pen, not a promotion. what actually identified the man was not a style of address but a patronymic: «gaspare de franceschi q.m ant.o ex hoc castro», which excluded two of three candidates outright because both were sons of a jacobo, named as such in their own baptisms. one word of kinship outranks any amount of inference from titles.
a spelling list is an instrument, and it belongs in the log with its counts

this archive searched a newspaper portal, wrote «zero in every spelling», and was wrong twice over. «every spelling» meant two. the two not tried were the two that mattered: de franceschi spaced, which reaches a whole journal the unspaced form does not, and defrančeski in croatian orthography, which is how a croatian paper actually prints the name. one of them found the moment carlo de franceschi was told to become a historian. the other found a man at ližnjan nobody knew existed. and one spelling had to be thrown away. franceski returns 1332 results because croatian ocr renders «francuski» — «french» close enough to match. a count that large is a language, not a family, and a sweep that banked it would have drowned in adjectives. the rule: record the terms and their counts, every time, in the search log — never in prose as «every spelling». a nil you cannot audit is not a finding, it is a stopping place, and it tells the next reader to stop too.
when the priest changes, the surname changes — and the index loses you

on 29 april 1782 this family stops being «defranceschi» and starts being «franceschi», and nothing happened to the family. the parish of svetvinčenat changed archpriest. d. antonio massalini had written the name as one word for twenty years; d. paolo cossaich writes it as two, without the «de». six weeks later he writes «capo antonio de franceschi» — «de» restored, spaced. three spellings of one household inside three months, and the household did not move, marry out or change anything about itself. ⚠ this is where a name-indexed search silently fails. a reader searching an index for «defranceschi» in the svetvinčenat marriages finds the family up to 1782 and then loses it — not because the entries stop but because the clerk's hand changed. the gap would look exactly like a family leaving the parish. so: a surname is a property of the scribe, not only of the person. before concluding a family left a place, establish who was writing the book on the date the trail stops — and read forward past it in the images rather than the index. this archive found it only because it was reading the film frame by frame. (the same lesson from the other end: a spelling list is an instrument, and the two spellings not tried are always the two that matter.)
a parish register records where the couple were, not where the parish is

on 13 march 1783 a svetvinčenat couple were married at parenzo, and the act is in the svetvinčenat book. «…furono interrogati da me sottoscritto nella chiesa della b.v. degli angioli di parenzo» — vittorio de franceschi and eufemia bergamo, dispensed from the three banns and from the closed season of lent, with witnesses from parenzo and ližnjan and none from the castle. (doc.) two things follow, and both are easy to get wrong. · a register of parish a can be the only record of an event in parish b. searching poreč's own books for this marriage would find nothing; it is filed at svetvinčenat because that is where the couple belonged, not where they stood. · the converse trap is worse: do not read the parish as the place. an archive that maps every act to its register's parish will put this couple at svetvinčenat on a day they were thirty kilometres away. the register usually says so plainly, in the clause nobody reads — the one between the dispensation and the witnesses, naming the church. it is worth reading every time, and this archive now does.
a name, a year and a camp are not an identification

on 29 september this archive went looking for a man who died at dachau, and arolsen offered one who matched on everything it had asked about. «defranceschi, antonio — 31 january 1909 — prisoner 8165.» the surname, the birth year, the camp system. three fields, all agreeing, and all of them fields this archive had chosen to search on. he was a different man. the record was an its cross-reference card, pointing to a file under defrancesco — born at moncalvo in piedmont, died at dachau on 7 february 1945. the man being looked for was born at gologorica in istria and died on 15 july 1944. two rules come out of it. · test on a field you did not search on. surname, birth year and camp were the query; birthplace and date of death were not, and they are what settled it. a match that agrees only on what you asked is not evidence — it is your own question handed back to you. · an index entry is not a document. the thing that matched was an archive's name-authority card, created to link two spellings. following it to the file it pointed at took one click and reversed the answer. read the document the index stands for before believing the index. ⚠ and the near-miss had a hook in it. the arolsen man was committed by sipo trieste and recorded as «italian, yugoslavian» — adriatic markers that made him feel right. a detail that fits the story is the most expensive kind of coincidence, because it buys the rest of the match. the birthplace was written four times; it governed.
grep the archive before the source, not after

6 october 2026. asked whether gračišće could be reached on familysearch, this session went and checked — and the archive had answered it on 15 september, in a row that walked all 3,488 collections, opened 44, and tested «austria, catholic church records» and «hungary, civil registration» by name against a control. stronger work than the re-run, three weeks old, sitting in the same file the re-run was about to be written into. and the second row written that morning was worse: it announced a familysearch waypoint for krbune as a find. the waypoint was already in six files — the worklist had carried it since 1 october. the cost is not the wasted hour. it is that a re-run written up as a discovery makes the archive look like it is finding things it already knew, and the next person cannot tell which rows are new ground. so: grep searched.json, sources.json and worklist.json for the source and the place before opening anything — not before publishing, which is too late to save the work. a re-run is still worth writing down — this one confirmed the september negative from a second dataset and added two parishes to the absent list — but it must be labelled a verification in its first sentence. verification is worth publishing; it is not discovery.
the roster is where findings go to be forgotten

6 october 2026. walking the death register turned up two defranceschi the archive had already documented — and in both cases the roster row had not been told. · maximilianus, dead at four in 1817: gologorica.json carried the death that morning; the roster row still read «no register has been read for this person here» with d: null. · josephus, dead 1838: the line data carried «born 4 march 1765», documented, and explicitly noted it as a correction of «about 1763» — and the roster row still said 1763, with an empty note. neither was caught by a check. check-propagation greps for retired wording; these were not wrong sentences but missing ones, and a missing sentence matches no pattern. both surfaced only because the walk re-opened the page and the roster was then read back against it. so: when a finding is written into a topic file, open the person's roster row in the same breath and look at it. a person page is the address a reader is sent to. if the finding is on the line page and not on the row, every link into that person still shows the old state — and the archive looks, from the one angle a reader actually uses, as though the work was never done. both rows needed re-declaration in data/decisions.json, and the gate refused the first commit until it got one, which is the system working.
look at the frame either side before calling a page read

this reel shoots some openings twice, and both pairs found so far had a defective first exposure. · pages 27–28 (1805): m01069241 has a loose slip of paper lying across the page, hiding seven entries; m01069242 has it lifted away. · pages 81–82 (1845–46): m01069269 is cropped at the left edge and the month column is gone — seven deaths dated «22, 4, 26, 8, 28, 12, 26» with no month; m01069270 is framed wider and gives martii, augusti, 8bris, 9bris, decembris. neither was detectable from the frame itself. the slip looks like part of the page; the crop looks like the page simply starting there. two automated attempts to find duplicates had already failed — ink coverage and pixel difference both scored a known duplicate inside the range of ordinary consecutive pages. so the rule is manual and cheap: before accepting a page as read, open the frame on either side of it. twice now that has been the difference between a page recorded as read and a page actually read. ⚠ it also means the coverage figure overstates: it counts frames cited, and a duplicate pair is one opening counted twice.
a section key is an id too — check before you mint it

6 october 2026. a new finding was written into gologorica.json under the key duplicates. the key was already taken, by the 1836 collation certificate — and json.dump silently replaced it. six paragraphs and a plate, gone, on a finding that had itself only been recovered after the crop-truncation error. nothing in the gate could see it. the json stayed valid, the site built, the links resolved, and check-story counted the same number of findings — it does not know which. it surfaced only because the next insert asserted its anchor occurred exactly once and that assertion failed. this archive's rule that person ids are minted once and frozen applies to section keys as well. they are published addresses: a reader scrolling the line page meets them in order, and a clobbered one is a deleted page with no 404 to show for it. so: assert key not in data before writing a new block, and when a key must be reused, diff the old value first.
a sentence about how a register names people is a claim about every page of it

6 october 2026. this archive published that a defranceschi had married a deprato — joining the two families it had spent weeks separating — on the premise that «these registers enter a married woman under her birth surname». the premise was backwards. they use the husband's. the claim stood two hours. what killed it was eight pages further on in the same book: «lambertina defranceschi, civis», who was born peschle. and the premise's own star witness said so all along — «catharina deprato nata rovisi … uxor joh: baptista» — deprato is the husband's family, rovisi is hers. that entry had been cited as evidence for the opposite, because it was read for its surnames and not for its grammar.* this archive has now made this mistake twice in one week. the first was a sentence about when the register stops writing latin — true of two folios, false by folio 98. both are the same shape: a generalisation about a book's habits, drawn from a handful of pages, and published as if it had been tested across the volume. so the rule. before a claim of the form «this register always does x», find three instances where the answer is known from outside the register, and say which they are. here the test was cheap and would have worked: two women in this very book have maiden names recorded elsewhere, and both are entered under their husbands'. ⚠ note what did not catch it: nothing in the gate can test a premise about a register's habits. it was caught by continuing to walk.
a wrong decade with the right day is a typo, not a namesake

6 october 2026. two rows in this archive carried a death year decades out, and both had been diagnosed the same way: «a gap this wide means one side is describing a different person's death — most often a namesake in the same parish». neither was a namesake. both were transcription slips, and the tell was sitting in the data all along.
this archive had the register gives
clementina 10 march 1840 10 march 1870
josephus 22 december 1857 22 december 1878

the day and the month were right in both. a confusion of two people scatters all three fields; a slip that preserves «10 march» and «22 december» and moves only the decade is a keying error. and in both the register's age closed on the declared birth to the month, which a different person's death would not do. so, before reaching for «two people of the same name»: check whether the day and month agree. if they do, the cheap explanation is a mis-keyed year, and the age at death will usually settle it against the known birth — no second person required. ⚠ both rows had also written down the right remedy — «this needs the burial register, not a judgement» — and it worked exactly as written, three weeks and two weeks later respectively. the lesson there is to work the worklist down: the wrong years were live on the site the whole time.
a house number is an address, not a household

6 october 2026. the gologorica death book's index gives at least six house numbers two households each — house 6 is both «deprato leonardus» and «sestan vincent»; house 9 is «berdar» and «peer»; and the same at 48, 55, 84 and 98. this archive had been using house numbers as if they identified families — «casa 31», «casa 36», «house 7» — and had raised a worklist item and published a claim it then withdrew over a defranceschi dying in what it called «the deprato house». the house was also a sestan house. three families at one address across seventy years, and house 28 held palmano, peer and flegar across eighty. so: a house number locates a building at a moment. to use one as evidence about a family it needs a date and, because the village was renumbered about 1806, a statement of which numbering it is in. without both it is not a fact about anybody. ⚠ the sharpest case: the archive's «casa 31», from the 1780s baptisms, is old numbering — and the index's «rabar alias tomelincich n. 31» is new. same number, different buildings, and nothing may be carried between them.
ask whether the register says anything about itself before reporting a nil from it

9 october 2026. the gračišće baptism book of 1667–1745 tells the reader, on folio 134, that it is incomplete. at the visitation of 18 july 1732 the vicar general wrote into the register that baptisms had been «omissa per negligentiam» — omitted through negligence — and ordered the ministers to recover them and write them in «nulla interposita mora». the decree is transcribed and plated in full. this archive had read sixty leaves of that book toward a nil without ever asking whether the book had an opinion about its own completeness. so, before a nil is reported from any volume: read the front matter, the flyleaves, the blank-looking leaves and anything in a hand that is not the usual one. visitation decrees, a new priest's note on taking over, a later hand's «nastavlja se», an index that does not match the entries — these are the register testifying about itself, and they are doc* of the strongest kind, because they come from the authority that could see the original. a nil from a book certified incomplete is still worth publishing. it is just a different sentence: not «no defranceschi was baptised here», but «no defranceschi baptism was written into this book» — and the second is the only one the evidence will carry. ⚠ it also qualifies the inference built on top of the nil. the direct-line page reasons from the absence of the surname as a parent to the family not having lived at gračišće. that reasoning survives — five occurrences and no residence across seventy-eight years is a real pattern, and the 1826 census says the same thing from the other side — but it now has to be stated as a pattern in the record rather than a fact about the town.
a thing catalogued is not a thing examined — grep the source's own title card, not only the surname

9 october 2026. this archive announced the discovery of two confirmation rolls it had catalogued nine days earlier — the film's title card says «matična knjiga krizmanih 1690-1694», and the frame map had carried it since 30 september. the existing rule is to grep before claiming a discovery: grep sources, searched and the roster for the source and the name. that rule would not have caught this, because the thing being claimed was not a person and not a document — it was a part of a volume, and the volume was already listed under its own shelfmark. so the rule gains a clause. before writing that any part of a source is unread, unexamined, unlisted or newly found, grep for: 1. the frame or page range, which this archive records in frame maps and reel tables; 2. the source's own title card or shelfmark — «signatura 3.1», «zm34k-215», «mkr», «mkk», «krizmanih»; 3. the native-language name of the record type, because a catalogue written in croatian will not match an english word: «krizmani» does not look like «confirmations», and that is exactly how nine days passed. the distinction that makes this worth its own rule: the archive's six earlier self-duplications were things it had found and forgotten. this was a thing it had catalogued and never opened. a catalogue entry is the easiest place in the world not to look, because reading it feels like knowing it — and an archive that files well will make this mistake more often than one that files badly, not less. the finding itself survived intact: the rolls had genuinely never been read, and reading them produced a real nil. what was false was the novelty, not the evidence — which is the usual shape of this error and the reason it is worth publishing rather than quietly rewording.
read every column of a ruled register, not the one your question names
